bullets: Systems thinking reveals that ignoring second-order effects leads to redundant work — teams using Bloomberg rebuild systems from scratch a year later when they overlook deeper leverage points.
Reliability and sustainability share more foundational vocabulary than commonly admitted — the overlap is greater than prior experience suggests.
Leverage points in systems are more fragile than assumed — two years of systems-thinking work has made practitioners more humble about where and how interventions truly take effect.
Sustainability efforts fail when they omit the second-order consequences of decisions — the most critical part of the system is often the one missed in early design.
The trade-offs around reliability cross-cut every domain — from software architecture to organizational behavior — and must be evaluated explicitly rather than defaulted.
Running a systems-thinking idea for two weeks is a practical way to test its validity — the rest of the process is iteration, not reinvention.
Bloomberg and IPCC are not just tools but frameworks that expose how teams internalize or misinterpret systemic feedback loops.
The most underrated aspect of systems thinking is the recognition that failure often stems from overlooked second-order effects rather than direct causes.
